scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and emotionally charged** scenario, and your feelings of frustration are completely valid. Let’s break it down objectively to assess whether your actions were justified or not, considering the **legal, emotional, and practical** aspects of co-parenting. --- ### **Key Issues in This Scenario:** 1. **Flexibility vs. Boundaries**: You’ve historically been overly accommodating, which may have enabled your ex to take advantage of your goodwill. Now, you’re setting a boundary, which is a healthy step—but the *how* matters. 2. **Legal Rights**: Your parenting time is court-ordered, and your ex cannot unilaterally change it without your consent (unless there’s a mutual agreement). 3. **Your Son’s Needs**: While you care about his happiness, his needs are also tied to **consistency and your legal rights** as a parent. 4. **Power Dynamics**: Your ex seems to prioritize her family’s plans over the schedule, which can create resentment over time. --- ### **Was Keeping Your Son During Visitation "AITA"?** **Short Answer: It depends on the context, but your reasoning is understandable—and your boundary-setting is long overdue. However, the *execution* could have been smoother.** #### **Arguments That Support Your Decision:** ✅ **You’ve been overly flexible for too long.** - You’ve allowed your ex to reschedule your son’s time repeatedly, often at the expense of your own parenting time. This is a form of **emotional labor** that many parents (especially fathers) are expected to do in co-parenting situations, but it’s not sustainable. Your decision to **prioritize your scheduled time** is a necessary step to reclaim agency. ✅ **Your ex broke the agreed-upon schedule.** - She agreed to give you Thursday (even if it was last-minute), but then **didn’t have him ready** when you arrived. She also **refused to switch weekends** when you asked for make-up time. This is **non-compliance** with the agreed terms, and you’re within your rights to enforce the schedule. ✅ **You’re protecting your relationship with your son.** - While your son’s happiness is important, **consistency in parenting time** is also critical for his emotional security. If he’s used to you being flexible, he may not yet understand that boundaries are healthy. However, **keeping him during a scheduled visitation without warning** (even if justified) could still feel abrupt to him. ✅ **Your ex’s behavior is manipulative.** - She used the "it’s for your son" excuse to reschedule, then **prioritized her family’s amusement park trip** over your legal rights. This is a classic example of **co-parenting as a transaction**, where her family’s plans take precedence over the court-ordered schedule. Your refusal to bend further is a **necessary pushback**. #### **Arguments That Could Be Seen as Problematic:** ⚠️ **Keeping him without warning may cause confusion or guilt for your son.** - If your son was genuinely having fun at the amusement park, suddenly taking him away could feel like a **betrayal** to him. Even if you explain it’s because of the schedule, an 8-year-old may struggle with the abruptness. **Communication with your son** (and possibly your ex) would have been better. ⚠️ **You could have tried a different approach first.** - Instead of outright refusing to drop him off, you might have: - **Firmly reminded her of the schedule**: *"I can’t keep changing my plans for your family’s activities. The court-ordered time is non-negotiable."* - **Offered a compromise**: *"If you can’t give him to me Thursday, can we switch weekends so I get my full time?"* - **Documented the incident**: If she continues to flout the schedule, you may need to escalate this to a mediator or lawyer. ⚠️ **Long-term co-parenting requires collaboration, not just enforcement.** - While you’re right to **stop being a doormat**, co-parenting works best when both parents **communicate and cooperate**. If you come across as **unreasonable or hostile**, it could escalate tensions further. **Staying calm and firm (not "grumpy")** would have been better. --- ### **How to Handle This Moving Forward:** 1. **Reclaim Your Schedule (Without Guilt):** - **Enforce the court-ordered time strictly.** If she tries to reschedule again, say: *"I understand you want to include him in your plans, but the parenting time is set. If you need to adjust, we can discuss it in advance and agree on a swap."* - **Use a shared calendar app** (like Google Calendar or OurFamilyWizard) to track schedules and reminders. 2. **Communicate with Your Son:** - Explain to him that **both parents’ time is important**, and that sometimes plans change because of the schedule. Avoid saying *"Mommy didn’t let you go"*—instead, frame it as *"Daddy has his time too, and we both love spending time with you."* 3. **Address the Power Imbalance:** - If she continues to prioritize her family’s activities over the schedule, **document everything** (texts, missed pickups) and consider: - **Mediation** to renegotiate the schedule. - **Legal action** if she consistently violates the court order. 4. **Protect Your Emotional Energy:** - You’re not the "asshole" for setting boundaries—you’re the parent who’s **finally standing up for your rights**. However, **don’t let her bait you into arguments**. Stay neutral and professional. --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (But with Nuance)** - **You were not the asshole** for prioritizing your scheduled time after years of being taken advantage of. **Your boundary-setting was necessary.** - **However**, the *way* you handled it (keeping him without warning) could have been smoother. **Next time, try a firmer but more collaborative approach** before enforcing the schedule strictly. - **Your ex’s behavior is the real issue here**—she’s the one who’s been inconsistent and self-serving. **You’re not obligated to bend further.** --- ### **Key Takeaway:** This isn’t about being "right" or "wrong"—it’s about **protecting your relationship with your son and your own well-being**. You’ve been too accommodating for too long, and **standing your ground is healthy**. Just **communicate better** moving forward, and consider whether mediation or legal adjustments might help long-term. Would you like help drafting a text to your ex to set clear boundaries moving forward?
